To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
T cells can acquire HLA-G1 through trogocytotic processes and that these regulatory cells are able to inhibit allo-prolificative responses.

(i) activated T cells acquire from APCs their HLAG-dependent regulatory function, (ii) HLAG-dependent regulatory T cells are generated through T cell activation, (iii) HLAG-dependent T cell regulatory cells act independently of HLAG.

HLA-G-exposing APCs induce the differentiation of T regulatory cells and that HLA-G1 is acquired from APCs by T cells through membrane transfers, which reverses their function to regulatory cells that act by expressing HLA-G1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
immune regulation, and more precisely, with the regulation of immune regulation.
the role of the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class Ib antigen HLA-G in the control of the immune response.
immune regulation by HLA-G, a molecule with immunosuppressive properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HLA-G is an important molecule in the regulation of the immune system.
Trogocytosed HLA-G1 molecules on T lymphocytes induce a new type of Treg cells that are capable of inhibiting allo-proliferation through HLA-G.
HLA-G expression by cells and tissues is not a mere passive phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Trogocytosed HLA-G1 can be used by T cells as a regulatory molecule to inhibit allo-prolifteration and that HLA-G can also be transferred to T cells by APCs, leading to the generation of a novel regulatory cell subset.
HLA-G-exposing APCs can generate regulatory T cells that act through HLA-G they acquired from these APCs or through HLA-G-independent mechanisms.
T cell trogocytosing HLA-G1 are "pretending" regulatory cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
trogocytic transfer of HLA-G from APCs to T cells is a mechanism of rapid immune regulation that is used in the presence of HLA-G-producing cells.
immune suppression can be achieved through a rapid cell-to-cell transfer of immunosuppressive molecules.
trogocytic acquisition of HLA-G by effector cells generates a new class of regulatory cells that might be involved in the regulation of immune responses.
